items.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010
items.q: The interviewee discusses the 'Dorian mode' as a musical concept, not a person named Dorian.

ctx.x: Well do you find it harder than, or a different kind of challenge to improvise like on a tune like “So What,” where you’ve just got two chords and they’re just —

Um hum. Exactly. I understand what you mean. Well to me it’s almost sometimes harder. For me. Because I mean just for the fact, well the more I study music the more I realize how many tensions are in there. See? At first I just looked at it as one thing. The Dorian mode let’s say. But no, it’s more than that. You start learning how you could — that’s the foundation. You could learn how you start building upon it. And I’m still working on that. Thinking about that. And then you could relate that to other songs…

change-change-change-change-change-change. And which I loved. But I’m saying but then when I got to “So What” I said what do I do? D Dorian for eighteen thousand years. And then it goes up a half step. But you know, but I mean, but to me they’re both great. But yeah, it does present a challenge, because that’s hard to resolve with all that movement with keys in the Songbook, that’s hard too. Because you’ve got to know your keys. But you’ve got to know your keys when you’re talking about superimposition on the…
